lawyer:
Abdul Baset Majumder with Md Hasan Rajib Prodhan, Advocates -For the Petitioner 
Nusrat Jahan, Assistant Attorney-General -For the Respondents
parties:
Sabedur Rahman (Md) ------ Petitioner
vs.
Commissioner of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Abdus Salam Mamun J: This Rule Nisi was issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 2-1-1997 vide Annexure-F and the impugned orders 15-11-1994 and 29-1-1996 vide Annexure-H and H(1) should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and as to why the respondent Nos.1-3 should not be directed to levy and collect customs duty, VAT and other taxes in respect of the said imported consignment on the basis of the C&F value.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Writ Petition are that the petitioner opened Letter of Credit being No.AGR/CASH/424/96 dated 24-11-1996 for import of 7 units of Used Vehicles as per C&F value, vide Annexure-C. The aforesaid LC goods arrived at the port of Chittagong on 30-12-1996 and the clearing agent of the petitioner submitted Bill of Entry on that date, vide Annexure-E. But respondent No.3 opened a file being number 4059/AP/ Group/10/96-97 stating in its para(2) that the C&F agent has applied for physical verification of the consignment for having no Model Code of these two units of reconditioned vehicle, vide Annexure-F.

3. On 2-1-1997 the petitioner by a letter addressed to the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong applied for assessment of customs duty and charges on the basis of C& F value of the imported goods stating also that the Yellow Book Value on those reconditioned vehicles were not applicable, vide Annexure-G. But by impugned Annexure-F, in paragraph Nos. 8-11 the respondent held that though the importer claimed that the C&F value was applicable in his consignment but failed to produce any documents in support thereof and that according to the order of the Board of Revenue the assessment of the reconditioned vehicles will be on the basis of Yellow Book Value excluding depreciations. The respondent thereafter has shown in "the said file the difference between the Yellow Book Value and the declared value of these two units showing that the Yellow Book Value of a TOYOTA CARINA Car ST-180 of 1838 CC manufactured in the year 1992 was US$ 4883.82 equivalent to Taka 2,34,738.11 but the importer has declared it to the customs authority at US$ 2200 equivalent to Taka 1,06,535.60 to be the Invoice or C&F value and there is a difference of Taka 1,28,202.51. In the case of TOYOTA LITEACE Micro bus KS 30G-QB 4486 CC and manufactured in the year 1991 the Yellow Book Value was US$ 2855.36 equivalent to Taka 88,182.19 and the importer has declared its invoice or C&F value to be US$ 1800 equivalent to Taka 55,886.24 having difference of Taka 32,215.91. Since there is a difference between the C&F Value and the Yellow Book Value, in the consignment the respondent has assessed duties on the basis of Yellow Book Value.

4. Thereafter, the petitioner invoked Writ Jurisdiction of this Court and obtained the instant Rule and an ad-interim order to the effect that "Pending hearing of the Rule, respondent Nos.1 and 2 are directed to allow the petitioner to release the goods covered under LC No.AGRA/CASH/424/96 dated 24-11-1996 on payment of duties and taxes thereon on the basis of C&F value declared by the petitioner within one week."

5. Mr Md Hasan Rajib Prodhan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that there is no provision in the Finance Act, 1995-96 and in the Customs Act, 1969 to assess customs duty on the basis of Yellow Book Value and that the impugned administrative Orders, SRO. have no legal sanction and are violative of the Customs Act, 1969. The impugned standing orders are Annexures-H and H(1) and I to this Writ Petition. He further argued that the impugned order of assessment is violative of section 25 of the Customs Act and in the consignment in question value means the normal value or C& F value alone and that the National Board of Revenue has no right to fix a value under section 25 as a whole and the impugned Standing Orders tantamount to denying the benefit of section 25 of the Customs Act and that the Yellow Book Value is much higher than the C&F value. Assessment on the Yellow Book Value is detrimental to the interest of the petitioner-importer and the invoice value declared by the petitioner was correct and he was entitled to release the imported reconditioned vehicles on the basis of C&F value.

6. The respondent No.1 has entered appearance by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition stating that the SRO No.215 dated 12-12-1995 has provided mode of assessment of duty of certain imported items on the basis of Yellow Book Value and the same is enforceable in law. In view of this SRO the petitioner was not entitled to release his goods on the basis of C&F value and that the National Board of Revenue issued this SRO No.215 in the greater national interest.

7. Mrs Nusrat Jahan, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent, submits that the Bill of Entry of this consignment was submitted by the agent of the petitioner on 30-12-1996 and the impugned SRO No.215 came into force on 12-12-1995 and, as such, on the date of presentation of Bill of Entry and assessment of duties and taxes on 2-1-1997 this impugned SRO Annexure-I(1) was in force. The Standing Order No.1653/96 dated 29-1-1996 has provided depreciation for imported reconditioned vehicles on year wise slabs. The petitioner was being aware of this SRO and other Standing Orders opened his LC on 24-11-1996 and was thus bound to pay duties and taxes on the basis of law prevalent on the date of presentation of Bill of Entry. The Bill of Entry of this consignment was presented on 30-12-1996 and on that date the basis for assessment of duties and Taxes were the Yellow Book Value in the case of imported reconditioned vehicles and the petitioner is stopped from denying it.

8. The learned Assistant Attorney-General next argued that the dispute between the importer and the Customs Officials on the point of invoice or C&F value and the Yellow Book Value of the imported reconditioned vehicles as the basis of assessment of duties has already been resolved and decided by the Hon'ble Appellate Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner of Customs, Chittagong vs Giasuddin Chowdhury and others, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 129. In paragraph 22 of that case, their Lordships have been pleased to hold that "The writ-petitioner's claim of assessment on invoice value and not on Yellow Book Value is a matter of interpretation and not a question of jurisdiction to assess customs duties. So the Writ petitioner has to pay Yellow Book Value before his goods are released."

Imported goods in that reported case were also reconditioned vehicles.

9. Relying upon this decision the learned Assistant Attorney-General contended that there is no scope for the petitioner to argue on invoice value of the imported consignment.

<u>10. The petitioner, on the other hand, submits that the Yellow Book Value is a stranger to the Customs Act, 1969 and not recognised by the Customs Act as a method of assessing duties.</u>

<u>11. We find that these arguments have thoroughly been discussed and dealt with in the case of Nasiruddin Ahmed and another vs Commissioner of Customs, Chittagong and others reported in 50 DLR 232 holding that Yellow Book Value shall be the basis for assessment of duties in cases of reconditioned imported vehicles.</u>

<u>12. In the interpreting Article 152 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh "Law" means any Act, Ordinance, Order, rule, regulation, by-law, notification or other legal instrument, and any custom or usage having the force of law in Bangladesh." So, we find that the Standing Orders, SRO, have their forces of applicability and Yellow Book Value was applicable in the case of the petitioner as mode of assessment of duties.</u>

13. Yellow Book is the book issued by the manufactures along with the vehicle providing its description and specifications together with manufacturer's and retail prices and accepted in the International Market, whereas an invoice is 'a written account of the particulars of goods sent or shipped to a purchaser, factor, etc with the value, or prices, or charges annexed generally issued by the supplier or the dealer. In the commercial transactions the supplier's statements or written account about description, specifications and price of the commodities is less dependable, for more than one reason that it could be varied, inflated or manipulated for the purpose of evading duties which is unfortunately, a common phenomenon in the field of Trade and Commerce. The manufacturer's book, called the Yellow Book, is more dependable because the manufacturer usually manufactures more than one piece of similar product considering its demand in the market and having same identification number called the HS Code, Model number, Engine and Chassis number of the batch and of same design and this is a lot of the same nature and specifications and amenities and they fix prices in the factory considering manufacturing cost and profit in view of consumption in the international market maintaining one standard of the same lot.

14. We find that there are provisions for depreciations in the impugned Standing Order to the benefit of the importers of the reconditioned vehicles complacent to their usability.

15. The respondent has stated in his Affidavit-in-opposition that the mode of assessment of duty on the basis of Yellow Book Value was introduced in the greater national interest. Greater national interest is the interest of the people as a whole and it mainly depends upon the persons to whom responsibility is entrusted to secure the interest for and on behalf of the people. If they practice the same in their management, conduct and discharge of official duties, the businessmen concerned to our utmost trust, shall also secure greater national interest.

<u>16. In the case of Federation of Pakistan vs Md Saifullah Khan, PLD 1989 (SC) 166 their Lordships held that 'Courts always keep in view the higher interest of the country while resolving matters of national importance in accordance with the Constitution and law. National interest must take precedence over private interests and individual rights.'</u>

<u>17. Learned Assistant-Attorney-General has lastly, argued that the Writ Petition is not maintainable on the face of efficacious alternative remedy provided by the Customs Act under sections 193 and 196. She has relied upon the case of Bangladesh and others vs Mizanur Rahman, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 where their Lordships have held that forum provided by the Customs Act for appeal against any order of the customs officials including the assessment order is an efficacious alternative remedy and the petitioner only on point of his grievance of assessment of Customs duties cannot invoke the 'Writ Jurisdiction. "Ordinarily Writ Petition against an assessment of Customs duty or imposition of fine is not maintainable and remedy of appeal is to be availed of against the same."</u>

<u>In the instant writ petition, except the Order of impugned assessment of duty there is no other grievances of this petitioner and, as such, we find that the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court Division is not available to a person whose grievances arise out of the order of assessment of customs duties. He has to prefer an appeal in accordance with the Customs Act, 1969.</u>

18. This Court by the ad-interim order allowed the petitioner to clear his goods on the basis of invoice value. Since we held that Yellow Book Value was applicable to 'his consignment as basis of assessment of duties and charges, the petitioner is therefore, directed to pay the balance duty to the respondents within 30 (thirty) days from this date and the respondents are at liberty to realise the balance duties after expiry of 30 (thirty) days in accordance with law.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.
